subject: mechanical
audience: FE Mechanical candidates and mechanical engineering students
title: The Turbine That Produced 1.2 MW From an Enthalpy Drop
featured_title: THE TURBINE THAT PRODUCED 1.2 MW FROM AN ENTHALPY DROP

presentation.challenge: The turbine power came from a 600 kJ/kg enthalpy drop, not from subtracting internal energies blindly.

practice.primary_question: How does an adiabatic steady-flow turbine convert an enthalpy drop into shaft power?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Using h2-h1 as positive turbine output or replacing enthalpy with internal energy for an open steady-flow device.

case_dna.target_misconception: For an adiabatic turbine, shaft power can be found from h2-h1 without regard to sign or flow-work effects.
case_dna.why_plausible: The inlet and outlet properties are often simply subtracted, and internal energy is more familiar from closed systems.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: Neglecting kinetic and potential energy changes, Wdot_out=mdot(h1-h2). With mdot=2 kg/s, h1=3200 kJ/kg, and h2=2600 kJ/kg, output is 1200 kW.
case_dna.corrected_model: For a steady adiabatic turbine with negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, shaft power out equals mass flow rate times inlet-minus-outlet enthalpy.

problem_statement: Steam enters an adiabatic turbine at 2 kg/s with h1=3200 kJ/kg and exits with h2=2600 kJ/kg. Changes in kinetic and potential energy are negligible. A calculation reports -1.2 MW because it uses h2-h1 as turbine output. Determine the correct shaft power output and identify the sign/model error.
fixed_constraints: Negligible kinetic and potential energy changes

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The turbine was producing power. The calculation called it negative output.
gates.prompt: Which enthalpy difference corresponds to positive turbine shaft output?

options.label: Wdot_out = mdot(h1-h2)
options.reason: An adiabatic turbine produces shaft work as the flowing fluid loses specific enthalpy.

options.label: Wdot_out = mdot(h2-h1)
options.reason: This gives a negative number for a normal enthalpy drop and reverses the chosen output-positive sign convention.

options.label: Use only internal-energy difference u1-u2
options.reason: Open steady-flow devices are naturally expressed using enthalpy, which includes flow work.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict turbine shaft power
gates.prompt: What shaft power output in kW results from the 600 kJ/kg enthalpy drop at 2 kg/s?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Read the turbine shaft
gates.result: The turbine produces 1200 kW, or 1.2 MW.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The first law closes the steady-flow control volume

cards.text: The turbine is adiabatic, so heat transfer is zero.
Negligible kinetic and potential changes leave the enthalpy drop as the available shaft-work term.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the turbine energy note
report: C1. Enthalpy falls from 3200 to 2600 kJ/kg.
C3. Therefore turbine output is mdot(h2-h1)=-1200 kW.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: With shaft work out defined positive, use inlet enthalpy minus outlet enthalpy.

evidence_choices.label: Wdot_out=2(3200-2600)=1200 kW
evidence_choices.reason: This matches the energy decrease of the flowing fluid.

correction.template: The turbine shaft power output is {power} kW.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Increase turbine output with the same mass flow and inlet state
gates.constraint: Keep mdot=2 kg/s and h1=3200 kJ/kg.

options.label: Reduce the exit enthalpy while maintaining a valid turbine process
options.reason: A larger h1-h2 increases shaft output in the stated simplified balance.

options.label: Increase exit enthalpy toward h1
options.reason: That reduces the enthalpy drop and power output.

options.label: Reverse the sign convention and call negative power more output
options.reason: Changing labels does not increase physical shaft power.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the turbine enthalpy-drop rule
gates.prompt: An adiabatic turbine has mdot=3 kg/s and an enthalpy drop of 200 kJ/kg. What shaft power is produced?
gates.explanation: For the simplified adiabatic turbine model, Wdot_out=mdot Δh.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the steady-flow energy balance
gates.confirmation: I confirm that turbine shaft output is tied to the flowing fluid's enthalpy decrease under the stated adiabatic assumptions.

items.label: What failed
items.value: The enthalpy difference was given the wrong sign for turbine output.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: An open steady-flow device is naturally analyzed with enthalpy.

seo.seo_title: Steady-Flow Turbine Power: 600 kJ/kg Drop Gives 1.2 MW | FE E-052
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Mechanical Case E-052: an adiabatic turbine at 2 kg/s with a 600 kJ/kg enthalpy drop produces 1.2 MW.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Mechanical turbine steady flow energy equation
seo.excerpt: For an adiabatic steady-flow turbine, an enthalpy drop becomes shaft work when kinetic and potential changes are negligible.
seo.direct_answer: For an adiabatic turbine with negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, Wdot_out=mdot(h1-h2). At 2 kg/s with h1=3200 and h2=2600 kJ/kg, the output is 2×600=1200 kW, or 1.2 MW.

faqs.q: Why is enthalpy used for turbines instead of only internal energy?
faqs.a: Enthalpy includes internal energy plus the flow-work term needed for steady-flow control-volume analysis.

faqs.q: What is the turbine power for a 600 kJ/kg enthalpy drop at 2 kg/s?
